steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Import the TypeScript type utilities that will be used to create a branded type for currency. Add the import statement at the top of the file.
steps.hint: You'll need to import from 'typescript' or use built-in TypeScript utilities. For this lesson, we'll use TypeScript's built-in type utilities that don't require explicit imports.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Importing type utilities
import { Omit, Pick } from 'typescript'
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have the necessary imports for TypeScript type utilities to create branded types.
successCriteria: TypeScript type utilities are imported or available for creating branded types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported the TypeScript type utilities needed for creating branded types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing the correct type utilities for creating branded types.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import the TypeScript type utilities that help create branded types.

steps.title: Define the CurrencyBrand type
steps.instruction: Define a unique symbol type that will serve as the brand identifier for currency types. Create a type alias named 'CurrencyBrand' that uses a unique symbol.
steps.hint: Use the 'unique symbol' type in TypeScript to create a brand identifier that cannot be duplicated.
steps.seedCode:
// Import TypeScript type utilities here

// Define the CurrencyBrand type here
steps.expectedOutcome: A type alias 'CurrencyBrand' is created with a unique symbol property, establishing a brand identifier for currency types.
successCriteria: The CurrencyBrand type is defined with a unique symbol property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the CurrencyBrand type with a unique symbol. This will serve as the brand identifier to distinguish currency types from other types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're defining a type alias named 'CurrencyBrand' that includes a unique symbol property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CurrencyBrand type wasn't defined correctly. Remember to create a type alias with a unique symbol property to serve as the brand identifier.

steps.title: Create the Money type with brand
steps.instruction: Create a Money type that brands a number with the CurrencyBrand to prevent mixing different currency values. Use a type alias that intersects a base number type with the CurrencyBrand.
steps.hint: You can create a branded type by intersecting a base type (like number) with your brand type using the & operator.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: branded type for temperature
type Temperature = number & { readonly __brand: 'temperature' };
steps.expectedOutcome: A Money type that prevents accidental mixing of currency values by branding numbers with the CurrencyBrand.
successCriteria: The Money type is defined as a type alias that intersects number with CurrencyBrand.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a branded Money type that will help prevent mixing different currency values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your Money type properly brands a number with the CurrencyBrand using type intersection.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Money type should be a branded type that prevents mixing currency values. Try intersecting a number type with the CurrencyBrand.

steps.title: Create a type-safe constructor function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'createMoney' that takes a number parameter 'amount' and returns a value of type 'Money'.
steps.hint: Define a function with proper TypeScript parameter and return type annotations. The function should return the amount cast to the Money type.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named createMoney that accepts a number and returns a Money value, providing type safety when creating money values.
successCriteria: The createMoney function is defined with a number parameter and returns a Money type value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a type-safe constructor function that properly creates Money values with the branded type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function has a number parameter and returns a value of type Money.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function named createMoney that takes a number and returns a Money value.

steps.title: Create a type guard function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'isMoney' that takes a value of type 'any' and returns a type predicate 'value is Money'.
steps.hint: The function should check if the value is an object, has a 'currency' property of type 'string', and has an 'amount' property of type 'number'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A type guard function 'isMoney' that validates runtime values and returns a type predicate.
successCriteria: The 'isMoney' function is defined, takes a parameter of type 'any', returns 'value is Money', and includes runtime checks for the Money structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a type guard function that validates Money values at runtime.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but it needs to return a type predicate 'value is Money' and include proper runtime checks.
steps.feedbackWrong: The type guard function is missing or incorrect. It should validate the Money structure and return a type predicate.

steps.title: Define a type-safe addition function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'addMoney' that takes two parameters of type 'Money' and returns a new 'Money' value with the sum of their amounts.
steps.hint: The function should accept two Money values, add their amounts, and return a new Money object with the same brand.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function 'addMoney' is defined that properly adds two Money values while preserving type safety.
successCriteria: The 'addMoney' function is created with correct parameter types (Money) and return type (Money), and it returns the sum of the amounts as a Money value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a type-safe addition function for Money values. This ensures that only valid Money values can be added together.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function takes two Money parameters and returns a Money value with the correct type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addition function is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a function named 'addMoney' that adds two Money values and returns a new Money value.

steps.title: Initialize test data with the constructor
steps.instruction: Create several Money values using the createMoney constructor function to test the branded type implementation. Declare at least two variables with different amounts.
steps.hint: Use the createMoney function you defined earlier to create typed Money values. For example: const salary = createMoney(5000);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have created multiple Money values using the constructor function, demonstrating how to initialize properly typed currency values.
successCriteria: At least two Money variables are declared using createMoney with different numeric amounts
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created test Money values using the constructor function. This demonstrates how the branded type ensures type safety when creating currency values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some Money values, but try to create at least two different amounts to fully test the constructor function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test values weren't created correctly. Remember to use the createMoney function to create properly typed Money values with different amounts.

steps.title: Test type safety with invalid operations
steps.instruction: Write a line that attempts to add a Money value to a regular number to demonstrate TypeScript's type error.
steps.hint: Use the addition operator (+) between a Money value (like testMoney1) and a plain number (like 10).
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see a TypeScript error when trying to add Money and number, demonstrating how branded types prevent mixing different types.
successCriteria: The code includes an attempt to add a Money value to a regular number, triggering a TypeScript type error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! TypeScript correctly flags this as a type error, showing how branded types prevent invalid operations between Money and plain numbers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're trying to add a Money value (like testMoney1) directly to a regular number (like 10).
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires demonstrating type safety by attempting an invalid operation. Try adding a Money value to a plain number.

steps.title: Use the type guard function
steps.instruction: Create a function named validateAndAdd that takes two unknown parameters, uses the isMoney type guard to validate them, and returns their sum if both are valid Money values.
steps.hint: Use the isMoney function to check each parameter, then cast them to Money and use addition.
steps.expectedOutcome: A validateAndAdd function that safely validates unknown values using the type guard before performing Money addition.
successCriteria: The validateAndAdd function is defined, uses isMoney to check both parameters, and returns their sum when both are valid Money values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented runtime validation using the type guard function to ensure type safety before performing operations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to use the isMoney function to check both parameters and handle the case where they are valid Money values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't properly use the type guard to validate the parameters. Review how to apply type guards for runtime type checking.

steps.title: Test the addition function
steps.instruction: Create a function named addMoney that takes two Money parameters and returns their sum as Money.
steps.hint: Define a function with proper type annotations for parameters and return type.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that adds two Money values while preserving the branded type.
successCriteria: The addMoney function is defined with proper TypeScript types and returns the sum as Money.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a type-safe addition function that maintains the Money brand.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function has proper type annotations and returns the sum as Money.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addition function isn't quite right. Check the function signature and return type.
